tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
A **polyhedron** is a $3$-dimensional shape where each side is a polygon. These flat polygonal sides are called **faces**.

**Prisms** are polyhedrons made of two identical polygonal faces (called **bases**) connected by equal parallel line segments. If these line segments are perpendicular to the bases, we have a **right** prism.

Let's take a look at some common prisms.

- A **triangular (right) prism** consists of two identical triangular faces connected by equal parallel line segments.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14230697/assets/9563bd4f9c40ff5921998ed5840f8e5b43fb1af579a64a06a14782be4a86ece2.png)

- A **rectangular (right) prism** consists of two identical rectangular faces connected by equal parallel line segments. Notice that each face is a rectangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14230697/assets/39ea3dd56722c7fb05ba275a054ff46479e3ee96851dafdd66fe09455a517f1a.png)

- A **cube** is a special case of a rectangular prism that consists of six equal square faces.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14230697/assets/415d03a9a886793eee4b4d16e50af26002c0881279481b2e70773b8b7bff02a5.png)

By adding more sides to the polygonal base, we can make more prisms. For example, the following shape is a pentagonal prism.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14230697/assets/8f4dd8fe8c120eabbe5a1ad6413f6f0cd9cd3d22efe8b13e25ac3d2a916f3258.png)

 

We can also construct hexagonal prisms, heptagonal prisms, etc.

tutorials.name: Pyramids
tutorials.problem:
**Pyramids** are polyhedrons made of a polygonal base, with the other triangular faces meeting at a single point. 

Let's take a look at some common pyramids.

- A **triangular pyramid** has a triangular base with $3$ other triangular faces that meet at a single point.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14230697/assets/d8597d1e526e2af72255f7dce1cc13e01cf76f1c53522003b126be67a0a6c55d.png)

- A **rectangular pyramid** has a rectangular base with $4$ triangular faces that meet at a single point. If the base is a square, we call this a **square pyramid.**

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14230697/assets/26700acaf9eae64227988ddcfb43269c0eba6f6447229ec8854cc1ebfeab3334.png)

- A **pentagonal pyramid** has a pentagonal base with $5$ triangular faces that meet at a single point.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14230697/assets/4c73b984b3e4a2ccb0796646ebb4c547947fab7359914599d928a63819818725.png)

Similarly to prisms, we can add more sides to the polygonal base to make more types of pyramids.

tutorials.name: Other Three-Dimensional Shapes
tutorials.problem:
Not all three-dimensional shapes are polyhedrons. Let's see some examples.

- A ** sphere** is the set of points with the same distance to a fixed point called the **center.** A sphere is a $3$-dimensional analog of a circle. A ** hemisphere ** is half of a sphere.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14230697/assets/84e7b63b5ec8761d4a3ac8a00b15a08f0dab7d4f95a536721df0c82e2999873f.png)

- A **cylinder** is a solid shape with two parallel circular bases. There are two types of cylinders.

A cylinder is **right** if the axis that passes through the centers of the circular bases is perpendicular to the bases. Otherwise, the cylinder is **oblique.**

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14230697/assets/f8ddb161d2d8628dd1294cc0d0042437300787217b518be73f010e79be90dcf7.png)

- A **cone** is a solid shape with one circular base and one vertex called the **apex**. There are two types of cones.

A cone is **right** if the axis that passes through the center of the circular base and the vertex is perpendicular to the base. Otherwise, the cone is **oblique.**

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14230697/assets/2f9e9ca18a36336ed99695bb51b167ffbd83f002139728f8dfe15227bf9f7745.png)

steps.title: Introduction
steps.html:
Introduction
?

A polyhedron is a -dimensional shape where each side is a polygon. These flat polygonal sides are called faces.

Prisms are polyhedrons made of two identical polygonal faces (called bases) connected by equal parallel line segments. If these line segments are perpendicular to the bases, we have a right prism.

Let's take a look at some common prisms.

  • A triangular (right) prism consists of two identical triangular faces connected by equal parallel line segments.
  • A rectangular (right) prism consists of two identical rectangular faces connected by equal parallel line segments. Notice that each face is a rectangle.
  • A cube is a special case of a rectangular prism that consists of six equal square faces.

By adding more sides to the polygonal base, we can make more prisms. For example, the following shape is a pentagonal prism.

We can also construct hexagonal prisms, heptagonal prisms, etc.

  • A rectangular pyramid has a rectangular base with triangular faces that meet at a single point. If the base is a square, we call this a square pyramid.
  • A pentagonal pyramid has a pentagonal base with triangular faces that meet at a single point.

Similarly to prisms, we can add more sides to the polygonal base to make more types of pyramids.

The solid is a hexagonal pyramid since its base is a hexagon and all other faces meet at a single point

Also, notice that:

  • The solid is not a hexagonal prism since it doesn't have two identical hexagonal faces connected by equal parallel lines.

  • The solid is not a rectangular prism since not all of its faces are rectangles.

steps.title: Other Three-Dimensional Shapes
steps.html:
Other Three-Dimensional Shapes
?

Not all three-dimensional shapes are polyhedrons. Let's see some examples.

  • A sphere is the set of points with the same distance to a fixed point called the center. A sphere is a -dimensional analog of a circle. A hemisphere is half of a sphere.

  • A cylinder is a solid shape with two parallel circular bases. There are two types of cylinders.

    A cylinder is right if the axis that passes through the centers of the circular bases is perpendicular to the bases. Otherwise, the cylinder is oblique.

  • A cone is a solid shape with one circular base and one vertex called the apex. There are two types of cones.

    A cone is right if the axis that passes through the center of the circular base and the vertex is perpendicular to the base. Otherwise, the cone is oblique.

steps.title: Identifying Spheres, Hemispheres, Cones, and Cylinders

EXPLANATION

The solid is a right cone.

Notice the following:

  • The solid has one circular base and one vertex. So, it's a cone.

  • The axis that passes through the center of the circle and the vertex is perpendicular to the base. So, it's right.
